anchors.paper_title: Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding
anchors.reason: Title and authors match the dataset exactly; the bioRxiv paper reports the uhd-EEG speech decoding study that produced this data.

metadata.methods_description: 128-channel EEG was recorded with a 10x preamp gain, together with bipolar EOG, EMG of the upper and lower orbicularis oris, microphone, display, and trigger channels (139 channels total). Each trial consisted of 5 repetitions of a single color word at 1.25 s per repetition, in calibration and online decoding sessions.

citation_details.title: Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding
citation_details.author: Motoshige Sato, Eri Hatakeyama, Masakazu Inoue, Yasuo Kabe, Sensho Nobe, Akito Yoshida, Atsushi Yamamoto, Yuya Kita, Mayumi Shimizu, Kenichi Tomeoka, Michael X Cohen, Shuntaro Sasai
citation_details.abstract: Abstract Objective . Speech Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a pivotal technology in facilitating communication for individuals with speech impairments. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) for noninvasive speech BCIs offers an accessible and affordable solution, potentially benefiting a broader audience. However, EEG-based speech decoding remains controversial especially for overt speech, due to difficulties in separating speech-related neural activities from myoelectric potential artifacts generated during articulation. Moreover, because paradigms for collecting covert speech data are inherently less scalable than those for overt speech, whether the neural dynamics underlying EEG-based decoding of overt speech are also present during covert speech remains an open and practically important question. Approach . Here we aim to delineate the extent of the neural contributions to EEG-based speech decoding, and the degree to which the underlying neural dynamics are shared across overt and covert speech, by employing Explainable AI techniques to a convolutional neural network predicting spoken words based on signals obtained by ultra-high-density (uhd)-EEG. Main results . We found that electrode-wise contributions to the decoding cannot be explained by their mutual information with electromyography (EMG). Furthermore, contributing periods of speech to EEG-based decoding are distinct from those to decoding solely relying on EMG. In contrast, there are significant overlaps in signal timings contributing to EEG-based decoding, regardless of vocal conditions such as overt or covert speech. Notably, the denoising process successfully enhanced the decoding contribution from electrodes within speech-related brain areas for all speech conditions. Significance . Altogether, our findings support the idea that, with appropriate preprocessing, EEG becomes a valuable tool for decoding spoken words based on underlying neural activities.
